$comment: Phase 47 (phase 40 carried item #5). The contract between the two places this app answers the
question 'does this row match what I typed'.
There are two, and there have to be. A paginated list cannot hold its rows, so its term goes to
the server and becomes `x.Column.Contains(term)` in a handler's Where. A Configurations lookup
already holds every row, so sending a request per keystroke would be a round trip that can
reorder against the typing; its term goes to `matchesLookup` in the browser. Phase 40 shipped
both and said plainly that nothing made them agree: 'they agree today; nothing enforces that
This file is what enforces it, in the arrangement phase 26b made for BsCalendar/bs-date.ts and
phase 39 for the two rich-text sanitisers: neither implementation is the source of truth for the
other -- this table is, and both suites read it.
The server half runs against a REAL SQL Server (Api.IntegrationTests, Testcontainers) and not
against the InMemory provider, because the two disagree about the only interesting property:
single-argument `Contains` is case-INsensitive on SQL Server (its default collation does it, not
the expression) and case-SENSITIVE on InMemory. A parity test run on InMemory would pin a
behaviour production does not have, which is the standing gotcha this file exists inside.
`haystack` is one stored value, `needle` is what the user typed, `matches` is what BOTH sides

cases.why: the ordinary case: a substring anywhere in the value
a prefix
a suffix
no match is no match
an empty term matches everything -- the unfiltered list
typed lower, stored capitalised
typed upper, stored capitalised
typed mixed, stored lower
a leading space is trimmed before matching, not treated as part of the term
a trailing space likewise
whitespace alone is an empty box somebody tabbed through, not a term
an interior space is part of the term
and so does not match when the value has no space there
a percent sign is a character the user typed, never a wildcard
and a bare percent matches only a value that contains one
an underscore is a character too, not 'any single character'
an underscore that really is in the value matches
a square bracket is not a LIKE character class
square brackets that are in the value match
Devanagari matches itself
a digit run inside a document number
a hyphenated fragment
